teaching_card.title: Research Summaries: Variables and Design (Hard)
teaching_card.body: Research-summary passages describe one or more experiments and then ask you to reason about how they were built. Sort every quantity into three bins: the independent variable (deliberately changed), the dependent variable (measured as the result), and the controlled variables (kept the same). When two experiments are compared, find the single thing that differed between them; that difference is the point of the comparison.
key_points: Independent = what the experimenters changed on purpose.
Dependent = what they measured in response.
Controlled = everything deliberately kept the same.
A zero or untreated trial is a control for comparison.
Experiments 1 and 2 usually differ in exactly one condition; find it.
To test a new factor, vary only that factor and hold the old one fixed.
A flaw is anything that changed besides the independent variable; reliability comes from more repeats, not fewer rows.
A conclusion about values never tested, or about a variable held constant, is not supported by the data.
teaching_card.worked_example: Students varied string length and timed the period, keeping bob mass and release angle the same. Independent: length. Dependent: period. Controlled: mass, angle. Experiment 2 repeated it in water: the only change is the medium.

screens.title: Three bins for every variable
screens.body: As you read the procedure, label each quantity: changed on purpose (independent), measured (dependent), or held the same (controlled). The table's first column is almost always the independent variable and the other columns are the dependent variable. Anything the text says was 'the same' or 'identical' is a controlled variable.
key_points: First table column = independent; other columns = dependent.

screens.title: Why a step was done
screens.body: Questions about purpose have standard answers. A trial with zero treatment is a control that shows the baseline. Repeating and averaging reduces random error. Holding a factor constant prevents it from confusing the result. Choose the answer that names the specific scientific purpose, not one that restates the procedure.
key_points: Zero trial = control = baseline for comparison.
Repeat and average = less random error.

screens.title: Comparing experiments
screens.body: When Experiment 2 repeats Experiment 1 with one condition changed, compare the two sets of results row by row. If the measured values differ in the same direction at every row, the changed condition matters. If they match, it does not. A trend that appears in both experiments says nothing about the changed condition.
screens.worked_example: Period in water is higher than in air at every length → the medium affects period. Period rising with length in both experiments is about length, not the medium.

screens.title: Designing the next experiment
screens.body: To test whether some factor affects the result, vary that factor and keep everything else, including the original independent variable, fixed. Changing two things at once makes the result impossible to interpret. To predict a new trial, place it between the tested conditions that bracket it and expect a result between theirs.
key_points: One new variable at a time.
A setting between two tested ones gives a result between theirs.
